description: cutText(text, maxUnits) returns at most maxUnits UTF-16 code units of text and never splits a surrogate pair: when the unit that would end the cut is a high surrogate (D800-DBFF), the cut takes one unit less. It cuts and does nothing else - no cleaning, no trimming, no ellipsis. A text that already fits comes back unchanged, and a maxUnits of zero or less gives the empty text.

Why: this contract cuts long text (a message at 200 KiB, a tool call's output at 32 KiB, a persona's core memory at 12,000 characters, a mark's note at 2,000), and a cut counted in UTF-16 code units can fall between the two halves of a character outside the basic plane. The half left behind is a lone surrogate, which a JSON writer turns into an escape that Postgres jsonb refuses and Swift's JSONDecoder refuses, and one of them blocks a thread's mirror.

Order: an executor cuts first and cleans what it kept (cleanText, fixtures/rules/clean-text.json). Cleaning text that is about to be thrown away costs for nothing, and a cut never leaves half a pair for the cleaning to turn into a replacement character. Both homes follow that order, so both write the same bytes.

The Swift copy cuts UTF-16 code units (String.UTF16View), not Characters and not Unicode scalars: one Character can be many units (a family emoji, a letter with combining marks), so a copy that counted Characters would cut somewhere else than this one. Kotlin's String.substring counts the same units. Cutting the units and then making a Swift String is not enough either: Swift replaces the dangling half with U+FFFD, so it would return maxUnits units where this rule returns maxUnits minus one.
Every text and every expected value here is well formed, so they are ordinary JSON strings; the inputs no JSON string can carry belong to the cleaning rule and live in fixtures/rules/clean-text.json.
